description: Estamos interessados em participar do evento da NASA e nos divertimos ao mesmo tempo que adquirimos conhecimento e experiência com projetos relacionados ao espaço, nesse caso mais especificamente sobre locais de pouso na superfície da Lua, possuimos conhecimentos de programação para tal, destacando Python, Java e Java-script e iremos dar o nosso melhor.

details:
Escrito para: os avaliadores do NASA Space Apps (em inglês, como o resto do projeto). O texto responde, na ordem, a cada pergunta do campo. Os números que cito são os do site.

LanderBnB – Lunar South Pole Landing Planner

What it does. LanderBnB answers two questions every lunar south pole mission must answer before landing: will the lander have sunlight for power, and will it see the Earth for direct communication? The user picks a landing site and a landing date. The app then shows, for the following 30 days (one full lunar solar day), the percentage of time the Sun and the Earth are above the real local terrain, the longest night and the longest communication blackout, a site score with an uncertainty range, and a classification (ideal / moderate / critical). A delay simulator shows how the outlook changes if the landing slips by 0 to 14 days. An hour-by-hour battery simulation tells whether a given panel, battery and power draw would survive the longest night.

How it works. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/JPL's DE440 ephemeris (NAIF SPICE kernels, via Skyfield) in the MOON_ME frame. We validated them against the JPL Horizons API to within 0.00005°. The terrain horizon of each site is computed from LRO LOLA polar elevation models (80 m and 240 m per pixel): 360 rays traced up to 300 km over the curved Moon. A body counts as visible when any part of its disk rises above that horizon. Because the Sun never rises more than ~1.5° above the horizon at the pole, which is comparable to the terrain uncertainty, every score comes with a ±1° range instead of a single number. Sites include the Malapert Massif summit, the Shackleton and Haworth rims, Nobile Rim 2 and Mons Mouton (the IM-2 landing site). The 3D Moon uses NASA SVS textures, plus a south polar cap built from the same LOLA data and lit from the real Sun direction for the chosen date.

Benefits and impact. Near the pole, a few hundred meters change everything: on the Malapert summit, moving 170 m changes sunlight from 66% to 77% of the time. LanderBnB makes that sensitivity visible, comparable across sites and explainable to non-specialists. Mission planners get a fast first-look tool, educators get an interactive way to show why the poles have "peaks of eternal light" and permanently shadowed craters, and the public gets an intuitive view of Artemis-era landing choices.

Tools. Python (NumPy, Skyfield, FastAPI), JavaScript with Three.js for the 3D Moon, HTML/CSS, pytest and Node tests (168 automated tests), Docker, and Hugging Face Spaces for hosting. The hosted site runs fully in the browser. The metrics engine was ported to JavaScript and tested to give exactly the same results as the Python pipeline.

Creative aspect. Instead of a static map, the app treats a landing site like a place you would book: "will it have power and signal during my stay?" The answer comes from real NASA data and is honest about its own uncertainty.

Factors we considered. Real terrain instead of a flat horizon, the uncertainty of the elevation data, the exact coordinates of each site (we derived them from the DEM when official points were not public), sensitivity to the landing date, and a design that is clear for both specialists and the public. Out of scope: Earth–Moon trajectory, ground-station availability and relay satellites.

AI assistance. Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding and research assistant: brainstorming, research, data validation, software development and debugging, documentation, translation, and parts of the visual design. The application itself does not use AI. All results come from NASA data and physics-based computation, and no AI-generated images are used.
